summary: 80 ft heavy steel tower built 1938 for the Tweed Fire District; the district's towers were decommissioned in the 1970s. No source describes the site today.

facts.agency: Former Ontario Department of Lands and Forests (now the MNR), which founded the Tweed Fire District

events.note: Fan-site list of Tweed Fire District towers gives White Mtn. as 80 ft heavy steel, built 1938
Wikipedia gives only the decade: in the 1970s all the Tweed district towers were decommissioned as aerial firefighting took over
Appears on Pembroke topographic map 31F, 3rd ed. (per firelookout.ca)

evidence.supports: White Mtn. is in the Tweed district list as an 80 ft heavy steel tower built in 1938
evidence.quote: White Mtn. (80 ft. heavy steel), Gull Lake (now known as Mississauga Lake- 80 ft light steel), Bruton (80 ft. heavy steel) and Tudor (80 ft. light steel tower relocated from Dungannon) Towers were built in 1938.

evidence.supports: The list heading places these towers in the Tweed Fire District, formed in 1922
evidence.quote: Tweed Fire District (Tower History Notes)- Formed in 1922

evidence.supports: The Tweed district was founded in 1922 by the former Ontario Department of Lands and Forests (now the MNR)
evidence.quote: The Tweed Forest Fire District was founded by the former Ontario Department of Lands and Forests (now the MNR) in 1922

evidence.supports: The district's headquarters served as the central hub for 21 fire lookout towers
evidence.quote: It was the central headquarters for 21 fire lookout towers

evidence.supports: The district's headquarters on Hungerford Road in Tweed served as the hub for 21 fire lookout towers
evidence.quote: The headquarters for the district were housed at Hungerford Road in town.

evidence.supports: Each tower took compass bearings on a fire it spotted and relayed them by radio to headquarters
evidence.quote: When a fire was spotted in the forest a towerman would get the degree bearings from his respective tower and radio back the information to headquarters.

evidence.supports: During the 1970s every tower in the district was shut down as aerial methods took over
evidence.quote: However, in the 1970s all the towers had been decommissioned as aerial firefighting techniques were employed.

evidence.supports: The fan-kept list covers towers still standing; it does not name White Mountain (absence checked by text search of the page, 2026-10-20)
evidence.quote: The Ontario MNR has decided, as of 2013, to remove many of these still standing towers.

evidence.supports: The index gives the location as Tweed, Ontario
The index says the tower is steel and appears on a 1977 Pembroke topographic sheet; the index holds no description of what stands at the site
evidence.quote: Steel. Appears on Pembroke topographic map 31F, 3rd ed., 1977

evidence.supports: The index has no notes or site description beyond its fields

notes_for_editor: The 1938 build date, the 80 ft height and the heavy-steel type come from one fan-site list (Geocities, Tweed Fire District notes). Firelookout confirms only 'Steel' and a 1977 Pembroke map sheet. The Wikipedia decommissioning sentence covers the whole Tweed district and reaches White Mountain only through the fan list. The index labels the location 'Tweed, Ontario', but its coordinates (45.17549, -76.63794) lie roughly 90 km northeast of Tweed village by my own estimate (not sourced), so the label may name the fire district rather than a town; check before publishing the location line. No photos found. Access and visit facts are omitted because no source describes them. The fan-site still-standing list is undated and its silence about White Mountain is weak evidence either way. Search budget used: 2. Fact-check 2026-10-20: all 10 evidence quotes were found on the first run. The story body is about 153 words. Changes: the Hungerford Road headquarters claim had no evidence entry, so Wikipedia's sentence 'The headquarters for the district were housed at Hungerford Road in town.' was added. The 'Tweed Forest Fire District' name in the first sentence was changed to 'Tweed Fire District' to match the fan-site source cited for the 1938 build. Three sentences that copied source wording were reworded. The still-standing entry now states what its quote supports; the absence of White Mountain from that list was checked by text search of the page on 2026-10-20, not by a quote. Caveat: the fan-site list says 'some of these towers were taken over by the Lindsay District in about the 1940s' without naming which, so White Mountain's status after the 1940s is unconfirmed.
